155.title: Kathina
155.hook: at the end of the rains lay people offer cloth for new robes
155.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, within a month after the rains retreat ends, lay people hold kathina ceremonies with processions and food, offering robe cloth and other necessities to the monastic community.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a day of mindfulness at home, and your line: a retreat at home. Is your quiet half-day on the calendar yet? Day one hundred fifty-five.
screen: `A DAY AT HOME — A RETREAT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Thirty monks set out to see the Buddha. They're forest monks from a town called Pava, and they've planned to spend the rainy season near him at Savatthi. But the start of the rains catches them on the road, six yojanas short, as the text counts it. The rule is the rule: stay in one place. So they spend three whole months stuck in a town called Saketa, close enough to picture him, too far to reach. When the retreat ends, they set off, through rain and deep mud, and arrive soaked, their robes filthy and heavy with water. What happens next, tradition says, is the root of a festival Theravada monasteries still keep after the rains. Today: Kathina.
screen: `THIRTY MONKS ON THE ROAD.` → `THE RAINS CATCH THEM.` → `THEY ARRIVE SOAKED.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook. The Buddha welcomes the thirty travelers, asks how their retreat went, and hears about the waiting and the mud. And he responds with a new allowance: at the end of the rains, monks who have kept the retreat may receive cloth and make new robes. That is the kathina. The word means firm, or hard, and tradition explains it as the wooden frame the cloth was stretched on for sewing. In the old practice, the whole community worked together, cutting, sewing and dyeing, to finish a robe in a single day. Here's the part that makes it a festival. Monks aren't allowed to ask for cloth. It has to be offered. So lay people do the offering. Within a month after the rains end, in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Cambodia, families and whole villages organize kathina ceremonies. There are processions, music, food, money trees hung with small gifts for the monastery, and at the center, a bolt of cloth. And notice who receives it. The cloth is given to the community as a whole, not to one favorite monk. The monks then agree together which of them will receive it, traditionally one whose robes are most worn. The rains began with staying still; they end with giving. Three months of monks practicing in one place, then a day when the people around them say thank you with something useful. Not money for its own sake, not a trophy: cloth, for the robe a monk wears every day.
screen: `A NEW ALLOWANCE: CLOTH FOR ROBES.` · `KATHINA — THE FIRM FRAME.` · `MONKS CAN'T ASK; IT MUST BE OFFERED.` · `GIVEN TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has been steady for you lately: a colleague, a neighbor, a teacher, someone at home. Think about what they actually use. Not a trophy, something useful. A meal, a tool, a warm pair of socks, an hour of help, a book they mentioned. Let one gift come to mind. Notice the gladness of planning it, the first of the three gladnesses you met in the giving week. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kathina. The robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains, named for the firm frame the cloth was stretched on.
screen: `KATHINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the rains end in gifts. Today, give something useful to someone who has been steady for you. Keep it simple and practical. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: your practice
156.hook: a morning bow, a sitting, a walk, metta, the precepts, a gift, the holy days
156.howItsDone: Many lay Buddhists keep a simple daily rhythm, such as bowing and chanting at a home shrine in the morning, sitting or metta in the evening, the five precepts through the week, giving to the monastery, and the major holy days through the year.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, kathina, cloth offered for new robes, and your line: the rains end in gifts. What useful thing did you give? Day one hundred fifty-six, the last day of camp three.
screen: `KATHINA — THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.`

segments.voice: On day ninety-seven, camp three began with four short phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Since then you've sat with sixteen steps of the breath, walked a lane of twenty paces, taken the refuges, met the five precepts, given without a receipt, bowed three times, lit a candle, kept the holy days, and learned what a retreat is. That's a lot of practice. Today we gather it into something you can actually keep. Today: your practice.
screen: `DAY 97: FOUR PHRASES.` → `BREATH, WALKING, PRECEPTS, GIVING.` → `NOW, SOMETHING YOU CAN KEEP.`

segments.voice: Camp three was built to add up. By its end, there's a morning, an evening, a week and a year. The morning is the one you built on day one hundred forty-four: a bow, the homage, the breath, a wish of metta, and a dedication of whatever good was done. Ten minutes. The evening can be the metta you learned for sleep, kindness sent out in six directions, or a short sitting of your own, with the hindrances named when they visit. The week holds the rest. A walk that's also a practice, on the lane or on the way to the bus. The five precepts, kept as trainings and taken again whenever one slips. A gift, small and wholehearted, with no receipt. And maybe, now and then, a quiet half-day at home. The year is the holy days: Vesak in May, Asalha Puja in July, the rains retreat and its three-month practice, kathina in the autumn, Magha Puja in February or March. The tradition itself has a pair of words for what we're doing. Pariyatti is learning the teaching: reading, listening, studying. Patipatti is practicing it: sitting, keeping precepts, giving. Camp two was mostly stories, camp three mostly practice. Tomorrow, camp four turns to the text itself: the Dhammapada, a book of the Buddha's sayings in verse, read in order, one piece a day. The practice doesn't stop when the reading starts. Each day's verse will come with a sit and a line to carry, so the words have somewhere to land. You already know how to sit. You know how to bow, walk, give, and begin again.

Evening: metta, or a sitting, or both? Somewhere in the week: a walk, a gift, one precept you'll pay attention to. Somewhere in the year: one holy day you'd like to keep. Keep it realistic, not heroic. When the sketch feels right, put it down and just sit with the breath, the way you've done a hundred times now. The bell holds the time.
Camp three close. A morning, an evening, a week and a year of practice, gathered into something you can keep.

157.title: Opening the Dhammapada
157.hook: 423 verses in 26 chapters, "the path of dhamma"; the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings
157.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Dhammapada is memorized, chanted and taught, and some Buddhists know many of its verses by heart; teachers often give a talk on a single verse and the story the commentary tells about it.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp three closed, and your line was you can do this. Is your week written down somewhere you can see it? Day one hundred fifty-seven, and camp four begins: the text.
screen: `CAMP 3 CLOSE — YOU CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: If you've ever seen a Buddhist quote on a poster, a mug or a yoga studio wall, there's a fair chance it was claimed to come from one small book. Some of those quotes really are in it. Some are not in it at all. The real book is short enough to read in an afternoon, and deep enough to keep coming back to. For the next seventy-five days we're going to read it together, in order, a few verses at a time, so you'll know exactly what it says. Today: opening the Dhammapada.
screen: `THE QUOTE ON THE MUG.` → `SOME REAL, PLENTY NOT.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada is a collection of four hundred twenty-three short verses, arranged in twenty-six chapters. It sits in the Pali Canon, in the part called the minor collection, but its verses are anything but minor in practice. In Theravada countries it is memorized and chanted, and some people know dozens of verses by heart. The name has two halves. Dhamma you know: the teaching, and the way things truly are. Pada is a word with several meanings: a foot, a footstep, a path, and also a line of verse. So Dhammapada can mean the path of the dhamma, or the words of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma, and the tradition happily hears all of them at once. Each verse is meant to be carried: short, rhythmic, easy to remember on a walk. Each chapter gathers verses around one theme, with titles like the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers, the fool, the wise, anger, happiness, the elephant, and thirst. An old commentary adds a story for almost every verse, telling who the Buddha was speaking to and why, and we'll meet some of those stories along the way. We'll read it in the translation Max Müller published in 1881, in the Sacred Books of the East. His English is old-fashioned in places, and when his wording and the Pali part ways, we'll say so. Tomorrow, verse one.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `PADA — FOOT, PATH, LINE OF VERSE.` · `A STORY BEHIND ALMOST EVERY VERSE.` · `MAX MÜLLER'S ENGLISH, 1881.` · then, large: `THE PATH, IN VERSES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Here are the twenty-six chapter titles, in Müller's English. Just listen, and notice which one pulls at you. The twin verses. Earnestness. Thought. Flowers. The fool. The wise man. The venerable. The thousands. Evil. Punishment. Old age. Self. The world. The Buddha. Happiness. Pleasure. Anger. Impurity. The just. The way. Miscellaneous. The downward course. The elephant. Thirst. The mendicant. The brahmana. Which one was yours? Hold that title gently, and let the breath take over. The bell holds the time.
Dhammapada. The path of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma: pada means both a step and a line.

158.title: The mind comes first (1–2)
158.hook: all that we are is the result of what we have thought; pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the ox
158.howItsDone: The opening verses of the Dhammapada are among the most often chanted and memorized Buddhist verses; teachers use them to explain that intention (cetana) shapes action and its results.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened the Dhammapada: four hundred twenty-three verses, twenty-six chapters. Your line was the path, in verses. Which chapter title pulled at you? Day one hundred fifty-eight, and verse one.
screen: `THE DHAMMAPADA — THE PATH, IN VERSES.`

segments.voice: Picture an ox cart on a dirt road in ancient India. The ox leans into the yoke and steps forward. Behind it, the heavy wooden wheel turns and follows, rut by rut, wherever the ox goes. The wheel has no say. It can't choose a different road. Everyone in the Buddha's world had watched that a thousand times. And the first verse of the Dhammapada takes that ordinary sight and says: this is how your life works. Today: the mind comes first.
screen: `AN OX CART ON A DIRT ROAD.` → `THE WHEEL HAS NO SAY.` → `THIS IS HOW YOUR LIFE WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here is verse one in Max Müller's English: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.” Verse two is its twin, the same shape with one change: if someone speaks or acts with a pure thought, “happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.” That's why chapter one is called the twin verses. The pairs mirror each other: the wheel and the shadow, pain and happiness. Müller's opening line is famous, but the Pali is even more direct. It says, roughly: mind goes before all things; mind is their chief; they are made by mind. Mind comes first. Speech and action follow. And what follows carries the quality of the mind it came from. The old commentary tells a story for verse one. A blind monk named Cakkhupala walked up and down one night and stepped on many insects. Other monks were shocked: he'd killed living things. The Buddha said no. He didn't see them, and he didn't intend it. There was no evil thought behind the step. For this tradition, what matters is the intention the act comes from. That's why the verse starts with the mind, not the deed. This isn't a promise that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything. It's closer to a warning, and an invitation. What you set going in the mind will be pulled along behind you. And you can watch the ox before the wheel starts to turn.
screen: `VERSE ONE: THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.` · `VERSE TWO: THE SHADOW THAT STAYS.` · `THE PALI: MIND GOES BEFORE ALL.` · `THE BLIND MONK: NO INTENT, NO FAULT.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath find its own pace. Now watch for the ox. A thought will come: a worry, a plan, a memory. Before you get carried off by it, notice what it's doing to your mood. Does the chest tighten? Does the face soften? Is there a small lift, or a small sinking? You don't have to change anything. Just see the thought step forward, and feel the wheel of your mood begin to follow. Then come back to the breath and wait for the next one. The bell holds the time.
The mind comes first. In the Dhammapada's first two verses, mind goes before everything; words and deeds follow, like a wheel or a shadow.
screen: `THE MIND COMES FIRST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the wheel follows the ox. Today, catch one thought steering your mood, and see where it was about to pull you. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: "He abused me" (3–6)
159.hook: hatred never ceases by hatred, only by not-hatred; this is an old rule (Dhammapada 5)
159.howItsDone: Verse five of the Dhammapada is often recited; teachers use verses three to six to show that resentment is kept alive by rehearsing it, and ended by not answering hatred with hatred.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, verses one and two: the mind comes first, and your line was the wheel follows the ox. Did you catch a thought steering your mood? Day one hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `THE MIND COMES FIRST — THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.`

segments.voice: Two in the morning. Someone lies awake, replaying it. What was said at the meeting. The look on a face. The perfect answer that came too late. The scene has been turned over so often it's worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket, and it still stings each time. The Dhammapada's third verse puts that replay into a single line, as if it had been listening at the bedroom door. Today: “he abused me.”
screen: `2AM. REPLAYING IT.` → `A STONE WORN SMOOTH.` → `IT STILL STINGS.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Müller's English: “‘He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,’—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.” Verse four is its twin: in those who don't harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. Notice where the problem is placed. Not only in what the other person did, but in the replay. The verse doesn't say the insult didn't happen. It says hatred lives on in the harboring. Then verse five: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.” Müller wrote love. The Pali word is averena, which means by non-hatred, by not hating back. It's quieter than love, and maybe more realistic: you don't have to feel warm toward the person, you just stop feeding the fire. The verse ends: this is an old rule. In the Pali, an eternal law. The verse presents it not as something new, but as an ancient rule. The commentary sets verse five in a story of two women whose rivalry ran on through lifetime after lifetime, each taking revenge for the last, until the Buddha stopped the cycle. And verse six belongs to a famous quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, who split over a small matter of rules. Verse six says, roughly, that people forget we all come to an end here, and those who remember it let their quarrels settle. So chapter one gives two tools for the 2am replay: notice that the hatred lives in the harboring, and remember how short all of this is.
screen: `VERSE THREE: THE REPLAY.` · `HATRED LIVES IN THE HARBORING.` · `VERSE FIVE: BY NOT HATING BACK.` · `REMEMBER HOW SHORT THIS IS.` · then, large: `HATRED ENDS BY NOT-HATRED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Now, gently, let a small old grudge come to mind. Not the biggest one. A mild one. Then, instead of replaying it, feel what it does in the body: the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. Breathe into that place. You don't have to forgive anyone right now. Just try not feeding it for the length of this sit. When the replay starts again, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
“He abused me.” The thought that keeps hatred alive, in verses three to six, and the old rule that only not-hatred ends it.

160.title: The wind and the rock (7–14)
160.hook: Mara overthrows the careless like wind a weak tree, not the steady; rain gets through a badly thatched roof
160.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the thatched-roof verses to explain guarding the senses and steady daily practice: small, repeated repairs rather than one great effort.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, “he abused me,” the replay that keeps hatred alive, and your line: hatred ends by not-hatred. Did you drop the grudge thought, even once? Day one hundred sixty.
screen: `"HE ABUSED ME" — HATRED ENDS BY NOT-HATRED.`

segments.voice: After a big storm, walk through a neighborhood and look at what came down. Often it isn't the tallest tree. It's the one that was already hollow, or shallow-rooted, or leaning. The old oak at the corner is still standing; the young tree with no roots is across the road. And inside the houses, the leaks show up exactly where the roof was already weak: the missing shingle, the cracked flashing you meant to fix in the summer. Storms don't make weak spots. They find them. Today, verses seven to fourteen: the wind and the rock.
screen: `AFTER THE STORM.` → `THE HOLLOW TREE FALLS.` → `STORMS FIND WEAK SPOTS.`

segments.voice: Verse seven describes someone living for pleasure only, senses unguarded, eating without limit, idle and weak. And Mara, the tempter, the figure who stands for everything that pulls us off the path, “will certainly overthrow him, as the wind throws down a weak tree.” Verse eight is the twin: the one who lives with guarded senses, moderate in food, faithful and strong, Mara can no more throw down “than the wind throws down a rocky mountain.” Wind and rock. The wind is the same for both. What differs is what it meets. Verses nine to twelve warn against wearing the robe without the inner change, and against mistaking what's false for what's true. Then come thirteen and fourteen: “As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.” And the twin: “As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.” The commentary tells these verses about Nanda, the Buddha's own half-brother. He became a monk on the day of his wedding, almost without meaning to, and pined for the bride he'd left behind. His roof leaked everywhere. But with patience and practice, the story says, he thatched it, and became known for guarding his senses. Thatching isn't done once. You check it before the rains, replace a bundle here, tie down a corner there. That's the picture: not an unbreakable fortress, but a roof kept in repair.
screen: `VERSE SEVEN: THE WEAK TREE.` · `VERSE EIGHT: THE ROCKY MOUNTAIN.` · `THIRTEEN: RAIN THROUGH BAD THATCH.` · `NANDA, WHO THATCHED HIS ROOF.` · then, large: `THATCH THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle into the breath. Now, like someone walking around a house before the rains, look over your own roof. Where does the weather get in? Maybe it's the phone at night. Maybe it's hunger, or tiredness, or one particular person who always gets under your skin. Don't judge it. Just find one weak spot, and see it clearly. Then ask, quietly: what's one bundle of thatch I could put there? An earlier bedtime. A snack before the hard meeting. Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
The wind and the rock. The same wind throws down a weak tree and passes over a mountain; the same rain leaks through bad thatch and not through good.

segments.voice: Your line: thatch the roof. Today, fix the one weak spot you found, with one small, practical repair. Day one hundred sixty.

161.title: Other people's cows (15–20)
161.hook: one who recites much but doesn't act is like a cowherd counting others' cows (Dhammapada 19)
161.howItsDone: Theravada teachers pair study with practice, and some cite the cowherd verse to warn that reciting scripture is not the same as living it.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wind and the rock, and your line: thatch the roof. Did you make one small repair? Day one hundred sixty-one, the end of the week and the end of chapter one.
screen: `THE WIND AND THE ROCK — THATCH THE ROOF.`

segments.voice: A hired cowherd stands at the gate at the end of the day, counting cattle as they come in. Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three. He knows every animal. He can tell you which cow gives the most milk and which calf was born last spring. But at the end of the season, not one drop of that milk is his. He's counting other people's cows. The Dhammapada uses that picture for a very particular kind of person: someone who might be a lot like us, a few weeks into reading a book of wisdom. Today, verses fifteen to twenty: other people's cows.
screen: `A COWHERD AT THE GATE.` → `HE KNOWS EVERY ANIMAL.` → `NOT ONE DROP IS HIS.`

segments.voice: The chapter ends with three more twin pairs. Verses fifteen and sixteen: the one who does evil “mourns in this world, and he mourns in the next”; the one who does good delights in both. Seventeen and eighteen say the same with suffering and happiness. Then nineteen and twenty, the cowherd. Verse nineteen, in Müller's English: “The thoughtless man, even if he can recite a large portion (of the law), but is not a doer of it, has no share in the priesthood, but is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.” Priesthood is Müller's word; the Pali means something like a share in the life of a seeker. Verse twenty is the twin. Someone who can recite only a little, but lets go of greed, hatred and delusion and lives it, has that share in full. The commentary tells it about two friends who became monks together. One studied, learned the scriptures, and had many students. The other learned only a little, went off to the forest, meditated, and became fully awakened. When the scholar came to test his friend with hard questions, the Buddha asked them both about the deeper stages of the path, and only the quiet one could answer. So look back at chapter one. The mind comes first. Hatred ends by not-hatred. Thatch the roof. And now: none of it is yours by being counted. Knowing verses is fine. It's how we're doing this. But the verse you live today outweighs the ten you can recite.
screen: `FIFTEEN: MOURNING IN BOTH WORLDS.` · `NINETEEN: COUNTING OTHERS' COWS.` · `THE SCHOLAR AND THE QUIET FRIEND.` · `CHAPTER ONE, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `NOT SOMEONE ELSE'S COWS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Let the four lines of this chapter pass by once, like cattle through a gate. The wheel follows the ox. Hatred ends by not-hatred. Thatch the roof. Not someone else's cows. Now choose just one of them. Not the one that sounds wisest. The one you could actually live today, in the life you have. Hold it for a few breaths and imagine one moment, this afternoon or this evening, when you might use it. Then let it go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Other people's cows. Knowing many verses without living them is counting cattle that aren't yours; living a few makes them your own.

segments.voice: Your line: not someone else's cows. Today, live one verse from this chapter instead of reading ten. Notice the moment you use it. Day one hundred sixty-one.
